math_plain: Rank search results by combining word-frequency scores from both the original query and AI-generated expansions, weighting each contribution.
why_math: Word frequency captures which documents best match what people searched for; AI-generated answers help identify synonyms and related concepts, so combining their signals captures more search intent.

math_plain: Learn to rank items by their predicted rating (1-5 stars), using the strength of past preferences to align recommendations with users' actual taste.
why_math: Strong preferences (5 stars) and weak ones (2 stars) reveal different patterns; including this strength makes the learner distinguish truly loved items from merely acceptable ones.

math_tags: finding the settings with least error
math_plain: Divide a geographic query region into blocks aligned with a grid so that each block perfectly matches the database's spatial index, minimizing extra unwanted lookups.
why_math: When query borders align with index boundaries, the database can fetch entire blocks without any overlap; misaligned borders force the database to fetch blocks and then discard boundary points.

keeping only the few dimensions that matter
math_plain: Compare documents by measuring how many words they share, using separate upper and lower bounds to skip candidates that can never be similar enough.
why_math: If two documents must share a threshold number of words to be similar, then documents with too few possible overlaps can be pruned without full comparison; tighter bounds mean fewer candidates to check.

math_tags: keeping only the few dimensions that matter
smart random sampling and averaging
math_plain: Encode frequent items with short codes and rare items with long codes, then compress the lookup table by using these variable-length codes instead of fixed-width entries.
why_math: Frequently accessed items benefit from short codes; rarely accessed items can afford long codes. Overall storage shrinks because the average code length is shorter than storing every item with the same width.

predicting the next item in a sequence
math_plain: When a user has few interactions, generate multiple diverse facets of each item's appeal and use those to fill gaps, so the recommendation model sees richer behavior patterns.
why_math: Repeating the same item many times wastes capacity; creating diverse sub-preferences from real items trains the model on meaningful variations without adding artificial noise.

math_tags: combining many weak signals into a strong one
learning a function from examples
math_plain: Merge the weights of a single-query search model and a conversation-aware search model so one model does both tasks without retraining.
why_math: Two trained models each captured patterns the other missed; blending their weights preserves both because the shared foundation makes their parameters complementary.

math_tags: measuring similarity as nearness in a space
spreading information across a network
math_plain: Extract named entities from documents, then smooth document representations using a network of entity similarity so nearby documents in the network are treated as similar.
why_math: Documents sharing the same company or location are contextually related even if their words differ; spreading this entity-level signal as smoothness makes the metric capture human-meaningful similarity.

math_plain: Learn to score each available search method for a given question, then route each question to the search method predicted to retrieve the best answer.
why_math: No single search method works best for all questions; learning per-question routing exploits that different questions favor different retrieval strategies.

measuring surprise and information
math_plain: Measure how much each recommendation model relies on item attributes by randomizing those attributes and observing how much the predictions change.
why_math: If predictions change dramatically when attributes are scrambled, the model is using them; if predictions stay the same, the model ignores them. The change size reveals true dependence.

math_plain: Store past decisions and their reasoning, retrieve similar cases at test time, and verify consistency between retrieved reasoning and new predictions to catch errors.
why_math: Earlier decisions contain valid reasoning you can reuse; checking consistency between memory and current verdict catches when the model contradicts itself, signaling error.

math_tags: weighting the parts that are most relevant
learning a function from examples
math_plain: Replace learned importance weights with uniform weights in a recommendation model and measure whether the predictions change, revealing if the model truly uses the weights.
why_math: If uniform weights produce similar results to learned weights, the model is not exploiting importance ranking; if results differ, it shows learned weighting is functionally important.

math_plain: Rank news articles by combining simple signals (user history, article popularity, topic) with fixed weights, no model training required.
why_math: Fixed simple rules can outrank learned models when they capture the dominant signals; rules scale faster and are easier to deploy than updating trained models constantly.

math_plain: When evaluating if a search method retrieved the best results, only count misses where the missed result was actually relevant to the query, ignoring irrelevant nearby results.
why_math: Search databases often contain irrelevant items close to relevant ones; penalizing all misses overstates failure. Only penalizing semantic misses shows true retrieval quality.

math_plain: For a query photo, combine results from database lookup, web search, and image matching to retrieve candidate locations, then use a language model to vote on the most likely GPS coordinates.
why_math: Different search methods find different clues; voting on the result lets methods specialize: web search finds text context, database finds visually similar photos, matching verifies alignment.
